lessons.title: Fractions: explain, then transfer
lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.prerequisite: The child can divide a whole into equal parts and use the 2, 4 and 8 times tables. If not, start by folding paper into halves, quarters and eighths.
lessons.materials: One sheet of paper, a pencil and this lesson. No purchase or other website is required.
lessons.teach: Fold a rectangle into four equal parts; shade three. Split each quarter in half. Six of eight equal parts are shaded: 3/4 = 6/8. Explain that the whole and the shaded amount did not change. Model 3/4 + 1/8 = 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8.
practice: A jug is 3/4 full. Pour out 1/8 of its full capacity. How full is it now?
answers: Each quarter was split into two equal pieces; the same shaded amount now occupies six eighths.
5/8: 6/8 - 1/8. This is not 1/8 of the water currently in the jug.
lessons.check: Without prompts, explain why unlike denominators cannot simply be added and solve a new example such as 2/3 + 1/6 = 5/6.
lessons.next: If the explanation is weak, return to paper parts. If sound, try 7/8 - 1/4 = 5/8. Recheck one fresh question tomorrow and a week later.

lessons.title: Reading: distinguish evidence from inference
lessons.subject: English
lessons.prerequisite: The child can read the four sentences below with help on any unfamiliar word. No prior mythology knowledge is assumed.
lessons.materials: Read this original passage: Amir paused at the dark doorway, then tightened his grip on the torch. Behind him, the wind pushed leaves along the path. He called his brother's name, but nobody answered. After a moment, he stepped inside.
lessons.teach: Model the difference between what is stated and what is inferred. Paused and tightened his grip can support apprehension, but the text does not state that he was terrified. Explain grip (hold) and inference (a conclusion drawn from evidence).
practice: Give two clues that he might be worried.
Does the passage prove his brother is inside? Explain.
Summarise the passage in one sentence.
Use grip in a different sentence.
answers: He pauses and tightens his grip on the torch. Other well-explained answers may use the unanswered call.
No. He calls his brother, but the passage gives no answer or confirmed location.
Amir hesitates outside a dark doorway, calls for his brother, then enters.
For example: She loosened her grip on the rope. Accept any sensible new context.
lessons.check: The child distinguishes a plausible inference from a certain fact and supports it with words from the passage.
lessons.next: Tomorrow ask for the meanings and a spoken summary without the passage. Then apply the same three question types to a short section of the current reading book.

lessons.title: French: one pattern, several new sentences
lessons.subject: French
lessons.prerequisite: No conjugation knowledge assumed. Explain that a verb describes an action and its form can change with the person doing it.
lessons.materials: Use these patterns: je parle (I speak); tu parles (you speak, one familiar person); il parle (he speaks); elle parle (she speaks); nous parlons (we speak). These are present-tense forms of parler.
lessons.teach: Show the shared stem parl- and endings -e, -es, -e, -e, -ons. Point out that written endings matter even when several forms sound alike. Use a trusted teacher/audio resource for pronunciation; this printed exercise does not supply verified audio.
practice: Choose: tu parle / tu parles. Explain.
Change il parle anglais to we speak English.
Which part is the stem and which is the ending in parlons?
answers: Tu parles: the tu ending for this regular -er verb is -es.
parl- is the stem; -ons is the ending.
lessons.check: Cover the examples. The child selects the correct form for je, tu and nous and explains that the subject determines the ending.
lessons.next: Tomorrow mix the subjects again. When secure, try the same regular pattern with aimer: nous aimons. Do not apply it to irregular verbs such as être without teaching their forms.
